video_title: Tom Lee and Dan Ives Explain Everything | TCAF 260
gist: Live on-stage conversation with Tom Lee (Fundstrat) and Dan Ives (Yorkville Ives & Co.) recorded the day before a Fed meeting the market prices at ~90% odds of a 25bp HIKE, with the S&P 2.6% off its high, semis in a ~19-20% drawdown, and Anthropic's Dario Amodei having just published an AI-safety emergency post. Both argue the AI capex cycle is mid-1997, not 1999: chip demand runs 13:1 versus supply, every $1 of capex multiplies 5-6x through software, cyber and infrastructure, and consensus earnings are 25-30% too low. Specific calls include Nvidia re-rating from 16x, an 80% chance Tesla and SpaceX merge by end of next year, Palantir up 4-5x over three to four years, and financials re-rated as tech on blockchain rails.

insights.claim: Tom Lee expects a Fed rate HIKE (priced at roughly 90% probability by futures) to trigger a major equity rally rather than a selloff, because delivering the hike removes the market's fear of future hikes while pessimism is already high and earnings are strong.
insights.speaker: Tom Lee
insights.so_what: Positions the Fed decision as a buy-the-event catalyst; a hawkish move that is fully discounted can mark a local low rather than a top.
insights.quote: So I think the probability of a massive rally starting tomorrow is really high.

insights.claim: Tom Lee argues the market has gotten cheaper in 2026 because earnings are up roughly 25% while the index is up only about 10%, driven by CEOs who cut costs through a run of black-swan shocks.
insights.speaker: Tom Lee
insights.so_what: Multiple compression amid rising earnings is the opposite of a late-cycle setup and supports adding on drawdowns rather than de-risking.
insights.quote: this year earnings are up 25% and the market's only up 10. So the market got cheaper.

insights.claim: Tom Lee's top-signal framework is that markets are never at a top when investors want P/Es to be low while earnings are rising, unless the underlying economy is a deep cyclical - and he classifies the current US economy as a low-volatility economy that deserves a higher multiple.
insights.speaker: Tom Lee
insights.so_what: A reusable test for distinguishing genuine tops from de-rating scares; argues for multiple expansion, not contraction, from here.
insights.quote: you're never at a top when people want PE to be low and earnings are going up unless it's a true deep cyclical

insights.claim: Tom Lee names only two bull-market killers: a genuine bubble (which would require the market to converge on a single AI model and capex going to zero) and monetary policy intervention, noting the Fed causes 80% of bull-market endings.
insights.speaker: Tom Lee
insights.so_what: Gives investors a short, monitorable risk checklist - watch model consolidation and Fed overtightening, not headline scares.
insights.quote: The Fed 80% of the time is the reason a bull market ends.

insights.claim: Tom Lee rejects the idea that record debt issuance and IPO supply are creating a debt bubble, because a debt bubble requires the cost of money to be so low that bad projects get funded, whereas data-center financing costs are already rising and the market is braking the cycle itself.
insights.speaker: Tom Lee
insights.so_what: Reframes rising AI credit spreads as a self-correcting discipline mechanism rather than the first crack in the cycle.

themes.theme: Chip scarcity and the capex multiplier

insights.claim: Dan Ives says chip demand runs at about 13 orders for every one chip that can be produced and that true supply-demand equilibrium will not arrive until early 2029 at the current pace, based on what he observes in Taiwan and Korea.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: If the shortage persists into 2029, semiconductor drawdowns are sentiment events rather than the start of a demand cycle rollover.
insights.quote: Demand to supply right now for chips is called 13 to1.

insights.claim: Dan Ives models a 5-6x multiplier across the rest of tech for every dollar of AI capex spent, flowing into software, infrastructure and cyber security rather than staying with chipmakers.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Argues the tradeable opportunity is in second-derivative beneficiaries, not just the primary semiconductor names.
insights.quote: for every dollar spent on capex, there's a five to$6 multiplier across the rest of tech

insights.claim: Dan Ives believes consensus is underestimating earnings by roughly 25-30% over the next few years, and that this is already the pattern of recent quarters, extending well beyond five or six companies to most of the Nasdaq 100 and much of the S&P 500 by market cap.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Systematic upward estimate revisions would mean today's contracting multiples are on understated earnings - a double-barreled upside case.
insights.quote: investors are underestimating earnings by probably 25 30% next few years

themes.theme: US-China AI race and sovereign data

insights.claim: Dan Ives claims that for the first time in 30 years the US is decisively ahead of China in tech, with US semiconductors two to three years ahead (America's third-rate chip still roughly a year ahead of Huawei) and hyperscalers and frontier models not even comparable - though he concedes China leads in robotics and energy.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: The US lead is, in his view, still underestimated by investors - and China's robotics/energy edge marks where the offsetting risk sits.
insights.quote: for the first time in 30 years, the US is way ahead of China when it comes to tech

insights.claim: Dan Ives argues that both blocking chip sales into China and slowing frontier model development are self-defeating, because China does not slow down and closes the gap either way - a view he attributes to Jensen Huang's own reasoning.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Implies export-control headlines and AI-slowdown proposals are bearish for the US complex and bullish for Chinese champions, the opposite of the intuitive reading.

insights.claim: Dan Ives identifies sovereign AI - enterprises and states refusing to let model companies access their proprietary data - as the biggest structural risk to the model labs, since he expects hundreds of models and eventual model commoditization, citing Palantir's Alex Karp and Nvidia as the loudest voices on the theme.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: If models commoditize while data stays captive, value accrues to data-owning enterprises and deployment layers rather than to frontier labs.
insights.quote: The models will eventually become commoditized. Sovereign AI is basically sovereign data

themes.theme: AI safety politics as a market variable

insights.claim: Tom Lee reads Dario Amodei's weekend AI-safety warning as overdue and constructive, arguing every industry grows ahead of its regulation and that AI currently has zero self-regulatory organization while roughly 38 anti-AI groups and data-center moratoriums are forming.
insights.speaker: Tom Lee
insights.so_what: Self-regulation is a community-relations tool that protects the buildout; treat safety announcements as deal-making with voters, not as a demand signal.
insights.quote: it's overdue actually because you know every industry that grows always grows ahead of regulation

insights.claim: Tom Lee's precedent for AI backlash is the wireless industry: handsets went from transmitting at one watt to 25 milliwatts amid brain-cancer fears and cell-tower bans, and federal legislation eventually ended the fight rather than shutting the industry down.
insights.speaker: Tom Lee
insights.so_what: Historical analog suggests AI backlash ends in accommodation and standards, not in a capex stop - so protest headlines are noise for long-horizon positioning.

insights.claim: Tom Lee sizes AI capex at about $800 billion a year heading to $1.1 trillion, explicitly rejecting a path back to $400 billion, and reads safety rhetoric as CEOs buying public permission to keep spending at that scale.
insights.speaker: Tom Lee
insights.so_what: A floor-and-trajectory number for the whole AI supply chain; capex going to $1.1T is the revenue line for semis, power and infrastructure names.
insights.quote: it's 800 billion a year is the capex and it's going to go to 1.1. I don't think it's going to go to 400.

insights.claim: Dan Ives says a slowdown by Anthropic and OpenAI would be a regulatory-capture move that lets software companies and startups narrow their lead, and points to software stock performance as the market already pricing that.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Frontier-lab safety pauses are a relative-value trade: long application/software layer, cautious on the pausing labs' competitive moat.
insights.quote: when you get to the penthouse then you stop the elevator so others can't come up

insights.claim: Dan Ives attributes Elon Musk's support for slowing AI development to xAI being far behind Anthropic and OpenAI on models, arguing no one catches those two absent a regulatory-capture moment.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Reads safety advocacy by trailing labs as competitive positioning, a lens for interpreting future endorsements of AI regulation.
insights.quote: Musk knows from a model perspective, they're way behind anthropic and open AI

insights.claim: Dan Ives names political grandstanding over data centers - not valuation or financing - as the single biggest risk to the AI buildout, arguing every project voted down hands the win to China.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Local permitting votes and midterm politics become the key monitorable for AI infrastructure exposure, ahead of macro data.
insights.quote: you don't want politicians that have flip phones and Blackberries determining your technology innovation in this country

insights.claim: Dan Ives calls the March 'SaaS apocalypse' - which put Salesforce, ServiceNow and most software names into 20-60% drawdowns without a single earnings miss - the most head-scratching narrative of his career, while conceding Adobe and Intuit do have genuine structural AI issues.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Separates the real AI-disruption casualties from narrative casualties, a screen for buying the next indiscriminate software de-rating.
insights.quote: narratives create the opportunities

insights.claim: The three largest cyber security stocks - CrowdStrike, Fortinet and Palo Alto - are up more than 100% on the year after an April Anthropic security product announcement briefly convinced investors the sector was obsolete.
insights.speaker: host (Josh Brown)
insights.so_what: A concrete template: model-launch panics in incumbent software sectors have recently been 100%-return buying opportunities within months.

insights.claim: Tom Lee says investors now understand software stocks are downstream beneficiaries of AI rather than victims, and criticizes the reflexive 'fire, ready, aim' behavior of zeroing out allocations whenever a scary narrative or Fed hike appears.
insights.speaker: Tom Lee
insights.so_what: Frames instant allocation kill-switches as a recurring, exploitable source of mispricing in large-cap software.
insights.quote: software stocks are downstream beneficiaries of AI. You know, they're not uh victims of a boogeyman.

insights.claim: Tom Lee's macro framework treats robots as a third productive input alongside labor and capital, arguing an economy that solves robotics could sustain something like 7% GDP growth without inflation because robots become consumers and taxpaying units that fund government deficits.
insights.speaker: Tom Lee
insights.so_what: If credible, it is the mechanism by which an AI-era Fed can tolerate far higher growth without tightening - a regime change for long-duration equities.
insights.quote: an economy that solves robots could grow without inflation

insights.claim: Tom Lee's key condition on the robot bull case is that physical AI which merely replaces human jobs shrinks the economy, and only a robot ecosystem that consumes and generates its own demand grows it.
insights.speaker: Tom Lee
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete test for whether robotics adoption is bullish or deflationary for aggregate demand - watch whether robots create input demand or only cut headcount.

insights.claim: Dan Ives calls physical AI - true autonomous technology, broader than humanoid robots - the golden goose, and argues it could be a bigger capex cycle than anything seen so far, with Tesla's robotaxi effort the clearest listed expression.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Sets up a successor capex wave to data centers, and names Tesla and Nvidia as the primary listed ways to own it.

insights.claim: Dan Ives puts over an 80% chance that Tesla and SpaceX merge by the end of next year, creating what he expects would be the largest company in the world by combining their data and AI technology under one roof.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: A specific, high-conviction corporate-action call with an explicit deadline - directly tradeable via Tesla and any SpaceX-exposed vehicles.
insights.quote: it's over an 80% chance by the end of next year that Tesla and SpaceX ultimately merge

insights.claim: Tom Lee sees large remaining institutional demand for AI because many fund managers still run underweight or zero AI exposure on the belief it is a bubble, with family offices and IPO buyers as additional untapped bids.
insights.speaker: Tom Lee
insights.so_what: Positioning, not valuation, is the marginal driver - underexposed institutions capitulating into AI is the mechanism for the next leg up.
insights.quote: it's very difficult to say this is a bubble because it's a structural story

insights.claim: Tom Lee argues the best financial companies should be re-rated toward tech multiples - noting JPMorgan already knows about 70% of its earnings on January 1 while Costco trades at 50 times - and that the coming rebuild of settlement for robot micro-payments runs on blockchain, making crypto a major winner.
insights.speaker: Tom Lee
insights.so_what: A re-rating case for large financials plus a fundamental (non-speculative) demand driver for crypto rails tied to machine payments.
insights.quote: today on January 1, JP Morgan already knows like 70% of its earnings without even like opening a branch

insights.claim: Tom Lee explains the endless relative decline of equal-weight consumer discretionary versus the equal-weight S&P as a classification artifact: discretionary is the catchall sector, and as spending migrates to iPhones (tech) and Costco (staples), the uncategorized residual simply shrinks rather than consumer spending weakening.
insights.speaker: Tom Lee
insights.so_what: Warns against reading the discretionary ratio chart as a consumer-health signal, and suggests classification-driven mispricings in names like Delta and asset-light hotel brands.
insights.quote: historically consumer discretionary is what you call the catchall sector

insights.claim: Tom Lee argues Nvidia at roughly 16 times earnings is set up for the same multiple re-rating Apple got when the market finally credited the App Store, noting Costco trades near 50 times and Walmart 48, and that Nvidia's multiple would jump to 50 if it simply charged a membership fee.
insights.speaker: Tom Lee
insights.so_what: Frames Nvidia's stalled stock as a business-model perception problem, with the upside coming from multiple expansion rather than further earnings beats.
insights.quote: you're paying 16 times and you're paying, you know, 50 times to buy Costco and 48 time to buy Walmart

insights.claim: Dan Ives argues Apple's lack of a data-center capex budget and its own LLM is now an advantage, expecting roughly 20% of the world to access AI through an Apple device and the install base plus new leadership after Tim Cook to drive an AI-enabled device cycle.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Positions Apple as a capex-free consumer AI toll booth, a defensive way to own AI adoption without funding the buildout.
insights.quote: I mean I think 20% of the world's going to access AI through an Apple device.

insights.claim: Dan Ives says Palantir can appreciate four to five times over the next three to four years on free cash flow, calls it a trillion-dollar name headed toward $200, and argues investors massively underappreciate how far its enterprise technology has moved beyond government work.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: An explicit multi-year price target and valuation basis (free cash flow) for one of the most contested valuations in the market.
insights.quote: this is a stock that could appreciate four 5x from here over the next 3 to four years given the cash flow

insights.claim: On an Anthropic IPO expected in October, Dan Ives frames it as a transition from model player to enterprise player evidenced by its enterprise sales-force buildout, while Tom Lee says it is hard to qualify as a Granny Shot and that the valuation argument is the same whether it prices at one trillion or five, so investors will likely need to own both it and OpenAI.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives and Tom Lee
insights.so_what: Sets expectations for a marquee IPO: winner-take-all pricing means position sizing across both labs rather than picking one.
insights.quote: if it if it's valued at five trillion, it's the same argument why it's valued at a trillion

insights.claim: Tom Lee says the revival of legacy hardware names like Cisco, Dell, Ciena and Corning proves moats last far longer than a 12-month horizon because of embedded customer bases and physical real estate that cannot be replicated, and that roughly 30% of S&P returns come from companies that did not exist 10 years ago while the majority comes from existing holdings.
insights.speaker: Tom Lee
insights.so_what: Supports holding incumbent hardware and value names through disruption scares; he says most of the path to S&P 16,000 is already in investors' portfolios.
insights.quote: 80% of what'll get us there is already in your portfolio

insights.claim: Dan Ives dates the AI cycle as a 1997 moment rather than a 1999-2000 moment, expecting a multi-year tech bull market punctuated by white-knuckle episodes like circular-financing scares and macro shocks.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: The cycle-position call that underwrites every other recommendation here - it implies buying drawdowns rather than reducing risk into them.
insights.quote: this is a 1997 moment not a 1999 2000 moment
